subject: math
intro: Apply the Law of Sines, $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}$, to solve oblique triangles. Pair each side with the sine of the angle opposite it, use $A+B+C=180^\circ$ to find missing angles, analyze the ambiguous SSA case, and compute area with $\text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$. Round decimals to one place unless told otherwise.

items.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $A = 40^\circ$, $B = 75^\circ$, and $a = 12$. Find side $b$. Round to one decimal place.

steps: Pair each side with the sine of its opposite angle: $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}$.

items.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $A = 35^\circ$, $C = 65^\circ$, and $c = 18$. Find side $a$. Round to one decimal place.

steps: Sides $a$ and $c$ are opposite the known angles, so use $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}$.

items.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $B = 45^\circ$, $C = 60^\circ$, and $b = 10$. Find side $c$. Round to one decimal place.
In $\triangle ABC$, $A = 42^\circ$, $B = 58^\circ$, and $a = 20$. Find side $b$. Round to one decimal place.

steps: Use $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}$, pairing each side with the angle opposite it.

items.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $A = 25^\circ$, $C = 110^\circ$, and $b = 14$. First find angle $B$, then find side $c$. Round side $c$ to one decimal place.

steps: Now $b$ and $c$ are opposite known angles, so use $\dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}$.

items.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $A = 50^\circ$, $C = 60^\circ$, and $b = 10$. Find side $a$. Round to one decimal place.

steps: Side $a$ is opposite $A$, but side $b$ is opposite $B$, which is not yet known. Find $B$ first.
Use $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}$ and solve for $a$: $a = \dfrac{b\sin A}{\sin B} = \dfrac{10\sin 50^\circ}{\sin 70^\circ}$.

items.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $a = 22$, $b = 12$, and $A = 42^\circ$ (an SSA configuration). Find angle $B$, and explain why only one triangle is possible. Round to one decimal place.

steps: Use $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}$ and solve for $\sin B$: $\sin B = \dfrac{b\sin A}{a} = \dfrac{12\sin 42^\circ}{22}$.

The supplement would be $180^\circ - 21.4^\circ = 158.6^\circ$, but $A + 158.6^\circ = 200.6^\circ > 180^\circ$, so it is rejected. Equivalently, since $a > b$, side $a$ is long enough to close the triangle only one way.

items.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $a = 9$, $b = 14$, and the included angle $C = 50^\circ$. Find the area of the triangle. Round to one decimal place.

steps: When two sides and the angle between them are known, use $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$.
Here $C = 50^\circ$ is the included angle between sides $a$ and $b$: $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}(9)(14)\sin 50^\circ$.
The area is about $48.3$ square units.

items.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $a = 30$, $b = 20$, and $A = 55^\circ$ (SSA). Solve the triangle completely: find $B$, then $C$, then side $c$. Round to one decimal place.

items.prompt: A triangular plot has sides $a = 11$ m and $b = 8$ m meeting at an included angle $C = 72^\circ$. Find the area of the plot. Round to one decimal place.

steps: Two sides and their included angle are given, so use $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$.
The plot's area is about $41.8$ square meters.

items.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $a = 10$, $b = 16$, and $A = 30^\circ$ (the ambiguous SSA case). Determine how many triangles exist, then solve each one completely (find $B$, $C$, and side $c$ for each). Round to one decimal place.

steps: Since $0 < 0.8 < 1$ and $b > a$, check both the acute and obtuse solutions: $B_1 = \sin^{-1}(0.8) \approx 53.1^\circ$ and $B_2 = 180^\circ - 53.1^\circ = 126.9^\circ$.
Both supplements work, so two triangles exist.
Two triangles: $(B \approx 53.1^\circ, C \approx 96.9^\circ, c \approx 19.9)$ and $(B \approx 126.9^\circ, C \approx 23.1^\circ, c \approx 7.9)$.

items.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $a = 5$, $b = 12$, and $A = 40^\circ$. Determine how many triangles are possible, justifying your answer.

steps: The sine of any real angle is at most $1$, so $\sin B \approx 1.54$ is impossible. Do not cap it at $1$.
Geometrically, side $a = 5$ is shorter than the height $h = b\sin A = 12\sin 40^\circ \approx 7.7$, so $a$ cannot reach the base. No triangle exists.

items.prompt: Given $A = 35^\circ$, $a = 7$, and $b = 10$, use the height test $h = b\sin A$ to determine the number of triangles formed. Justify your classification.
items.answer: Two triangles, because $h \approx 5.7$ and $h < a < b$.

steps: Compute the height from $C$ to side $c$: $h = b\sin A = 10\sin 35^\circ \approx 10(0.5736) \approx 5.7$.
Compare the given side $a = 7$ to $h$ and to $b$: here $h \approx 5.7$, $a = 7$, $b = 10$, so $h < a < b$.
In SSA with $a$ opposite the given angle, when $h < a < b$ the side $a$ can swing to meet the base in two distinct positions.

items.prompt: Two observers stand $500$ m apart on level ground and sight a balloon directly above the line between them. From the first observer the angle along the ground to the balloon's line of sight is $65^\circ$; from the second it is $80^\circ$. Find the straight-line distance from the first observer to the balloon. Round to one decimal place.

steps: Model the observers and balloon as a triangle. The two ground angles are $65^\circ$ and $80^\circ$, so the angle at the balloon is $180^\circ - 65^\circ - 80^\circ = 35^\circ$.
The $500$ m baseline is opposite the $35^\circ$ angle at the balloon. The distance from the first observer is opposite the $80^\circ$ angle at the second observer.
By the Law of Sines: $\dfrac{d}{\sin 80^\circ} = \dfrac{500}{\sin 35^\circ}$, so $d = \dfrac{500\sin 80^\circ}{\sin 35^\circ}$.
The first observer is about $858.5$ m from the balloon.

items.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $a = 12$, $b = 18$, and $A = 33^\circ$. Determine how many triangles exist. Then, for the triangle in which angle $B$ is acute, find $B$, $C$, side $c$, and the area of that triangle. Round to one decimal place.
items.answer: Two triangles exist. For the acute-$B$ triangle: $B \approx 54.8^\circ$, $C \approx 92.2^\circ$, $c \approx 22.0$, area $\approx 107.9$ square units.

steps: Since $0 < 0.8170 < 1$ and $b > a$, both the acute angle $B_1 = \sin^{-1}(0.8170) \approx 54.8^\circ$ and the obtuse supplement $B_2 = 125.2^\circ$ must be tested.
Acute case: $A + B_1 = 33^\circ + 54.8^\circ = 87.8^\circ < 180^\circ$, valid. Obtuse case: $A + B_2 = 33^\circ + 125.2^\circ = 158.2^\circ < 180^\circ$, also valid. So two triangles exist.
Find the area with the included angle $B$ between sides $a$ and $c$: $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}ac\sin B = \dfrac{1}{2}(12)(22.0)\sin 54.8^\circ \approx 132(0.8175) \approx 107.9$.
Two triangles; the acute-$B$ one has $B \approx 54.8^\circ$, $C \approx 92.2^\circ$, $c \approx 22.0$, area $\approx 107.9$ square units.
